explanations.explanation: Ziklag it is, friend. These first helpers come to David there while he's still banished from the presence of Saul, Israel's king (1 Chronicles 12:1). David is out in the cold with no palace and no crowd, and men start walking in anyway. That's a good day for a banished man.

Gath doesn't show up in this verse. The text says these men come to David at Ziklag, while he's banished from Saul, Israel's king. A town name that sounds right is easy to grab. I once reached for a cooling rack when I wanted a rolling pin, so I'm not judging.

Bethel isn't the place here. The text puts these helpers at Ziklag, where David is still banished from Saul, Israel's king (1 Chronicles 12:1). Hold on to Ziklag, because it comes back later in the passage.

explanations.answer: They use both right and left hands
explanations.explanation: Both hands, friend. The text says they're archers who can use the right hand and the left to sling stones and shoot arrows (1 Chronicles 12:2). Nobody has a weak side. I've got one mustache for everything and I STILL drop the cookie box.

explanations.answer: They shoot from the backs of horses
explanations.explanation: No horses in this verse. The text says these archers use both the right and left hands to sling stones and shoot arrows (1 Chronicles 12:2). That's what makes them stand out. Two good hands, no waiting around for the favorite one.

explanations.answer: They can hit targets in the dark
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions the dark here. What it says is that they use both the right and left hands to sling stones and shoot arrows (1 Chronicles 12:2). Being able to do the job with either hand is the standout detail.
True. The text calls them Saul's kinsmen from Benjamin (1 Chronicles 12:2). These are men from Saul's own family line, and they walk over to the banished David. I think that took some nerve.

It's true, actually. The text says these archers were Saul's kinsmen from Benjamin (1 Chronicles 12:2). That means they came from Saul's own family line to join David. Hold onto that detail, because Benjamin comes up again.
Spear, friend. These Gadites are experts with the shield and spear (1 Chronicles 12:8). That's a pair you can count on: one to block and one to poke. Same as my oven mitts and my spatula.

Swords are a fair guess, but the text says shield and spear. These Gadites are called mighty men of valor, trained for battle, experts with the shield and spear (1 Chronicles 12:8). The spear is the other half of the pair.
No axes in this verse. The text says these Gadites were experts with the shield and spear (1 Chronicles 12:8). They were trained for battle, and the spear is the one that goes with the shield.

explanations.answer: A match for a hundred men
explanations.explanation: A hundred, friend. The least of these Gadite commanders was a match for a hundred, and the greatest for a thousand (1 Chronicles 12:14). That's the LEAST of them. I can barely match a hundred crumbs on my counter.
Ten is far too low. The text says the least of these Gadite commanders was a match for a hundred (1 Chronicles 12:14). The greatest of them was a match for a thousand. Think about that for a second.

Closer, but the text goes higher. The least of these Gadite commanders was a match for a hundred, and the greatest for a thousand (1 Chronicles 12:14). Even the smallest number on the list beats fifty by double.
Not quite. The text says they crossed the Jordan in the first month when it was overflowing all its banks (1 Chronicles 12:15). That's not low and not calm. That's a river with no room left.

False is right. These Gadites crossed the Jordan in the first month when it was overflowing all its banks (1 Chronicles 12:15). That is a river at full tilt, and they crossed it anyway. I get nervous when my timer gets loud.

explanations.answer: Whether they came in peace or to betray him
explanations.explanation: Peace or betrayal, friend. David says, “If you have come to me in peace to help me, my heart will be united with you…” (1 Chronicles 12:17). He's asking before he opens the door. That's wise, and I wish I'd asked every stranger who came near my cookie jar.

explanations.answer: Whether they had fought the Philistines before
explanations.explanation: David doesn't ask about the Philistines here. He asks if they came in peace to help him or to betray him (1 Chronicles 12:17). He wants to know about their hearts first. Their fighting record isn't the question.

explanations.answer: Whether they could use a sling and a bow
explanations.explanation: Slings and bows came up earlier with the archers at Ziklag, but not here. David asks whether these men came in peace to help him or to betray him (1 Chronicles 12:17). His question is about their hearts, not their skills.

Not quite. David says that if they came to betray him when his hands are free of violence, “may the God of our fathers see it and judge you” (1 Chronicles 12:17). He doesn't say he'll strike them down himself. He puts the matter in God's hands.

False is right. David says, “…may the God of our fathers see it and judge you” (1 Chronicles 12:17). He says it as a man whose hands are free of violence. He leaves the judging to God and doesn't promise to do it himself.

explanations.answer: We are yours and we are with you
explanations.explanation: That's what he says, friend. Amasai, chief of the Thirty, says, “We are yours, O David! We are with you, O son of Jesse!” (1 Chronicles 12:18). The Spirit came upon him and there's no hesitation at all. I wish I could sound that sure when someone asks if I want another cookie.

explanations.answer: We will wait and see what Saul does
explanations.explanation: There's no waiting in his answer. Amasai, chief of the Thirty, says, “We are yours, O David! We are with you, O son of Jesse!” (1 Chronicles 12:18). The Spirit came upon him, and he spoke plainly for them all.

explanations.answer: We came to ask you for land
explanations.explanation: Land never comes up. Amasai, chief of the Thirty, says, “We are yours, O David! We are with you, O son of Jesse!” (1 Chronicles 12:18). The Spirit came upon him, and what he offers is loyalty.

God, friend. Amasai says, “Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers, for your God helps you.” (1 Chronicles 12:18). The reason for the peace is that God helps David. And Amasai says it with the Spirit upon him.
Not the army. Amasai says, “…for your God helps you.” (1 Chronicles 12:18). The reason he gives is God, and that's the reason for the peace he wishes David and his helpers.
Family isn't what he says. Amasai says, “Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers, for your God helps you.” (1 Chronicles 12:18). God is the one he names as David's help.

True. The text says David received them and made them leaders of his troops (1 Chronicles 12:18). A moment ago he was asking if they came to betray him. After Amasai's answer, he gives them leadership.

It's true, actually. After Amasai speaks, David received them and made them leaders of his troops (1 Chronicles 12:18). So he welcomed them and put them in charge. That's a warm welcome, and I should know about warm welcomes.

explanations.answer: They fear he'll switch back to Saul
explanations.explanation: That's the fear, friend. The Philistine rulers, leaders of a people at war with Saul, say, “It will cost us our heads if he defects to his master Saul.” (1 Chronicles 12:19). They're worried about their own heads. I think nobody wants to bet their neck on a guy who might change sides.

explanations.answer: They think his men are too few
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. The Philistine rulers, leaders of a people at war with Saul, say, “It will cost us our heads if he defects to his master Saul.” (1 Chronicles 12:19). Their worry is about David going back to Saul, not about numbers.

explanations.answer: They want him to guard their cities
explanations.explanation: Guarding cities isn't in the verse. The Philistine rulers, leaders of a people at war with Saul, say, “It will cost us our heads if he defects to his master Saul.” (1 Chronicles 12:19). That's the reason the text gives for sending David away.

The raiders, friend. These Manasseh chiefs helped David against the raiders, for they were all mighty men of valor and commanders in the army (1 Chronicles 12:21). They came to Ziklag and got to work. Good help doesn't stand around asking where the broom is.

Not the Philistines here. The text says the Manasseh chiefs helped David against the raiders (1 Chronicles 12:21). They were mighty men of valor and army commanders. So raiders are the ones they faced.

The Moabites don't appear in this verse. The text says these Manasseh chiefs helped David against the raiders (1 Chronicles 12:21). They were mighty men of valor and commanders in the army, and they stepped in right when David needed them.

The army of God. The text says men came to David day after day to help him, “until he had a great army, like the army of God.” (1 Chronicles 12:22). It grew a few at a time, one arrival after another. That's how my own bakery got busy, one hungry baker at a time.
Pharaoh isn't mentioned here. The text says men came to David day after day until he had a great army, “like the army of God.” (1 Chronicles 12:22). That's the comparison the writer picks.

The Philistines are named in this passage, but not for this comparison. The text says David's army grew day after day until it was “like the army of God.” (1 Chronicles 12:22). That's the picture the writer gives.

explanations.answer: To turn Saul's kingdom over to him
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. The text says these men came to David at Hebron to turn Saul's kingdom over to him (1 Chronicles 12:23). They came with everything they had for the job. A crowd with one purpose is a beautiful thing.

explanations.answer: To win back the town of Ziklag
explanations.explanation: Ziklag isn't the reason this time. The text says the armed men came to David at Hebron to turn Saul's kingdom over to him (1 Chronicles 12:23). The mission was the kingdom itself.
The Philistines aren't the mission here. These armed men came to David at Hebron to turn Saul's kingdom over to him (1 Chronicles 12:23). That's the purpose the text gives.

True. The text says these men came to turn Saul's kingdom over to David “in accordance with the word of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 12:23). It's not just a crowd with a plan. The writer ties it to what the LORD had said.

It's true, actually. The text says they came to Hebron to turn Saul's kingdom over to David “in accordance with the word of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 12:23). The writer says it right in the verse. It's easy to read past that line when the crowd is so big.

All Israel, friend. The text says these men of war came to Hebron fully determined to make David king over all Israel (1 Chronicles 12:38). They didn't come to crown him over one tribe. They came for the whole nation.

Judah alone is too small. The text says these men came to Hebron fully determined to make David king over all Israel (1 Chronicles 12:38). Judah was only one of the tribes that sent men, and the whole list stretches much wider.

Benjamin alone isn't it. The text says they came fully determined to make David king over all Israel (1 Chronicles 12:38). Benjamin is on the list, but so are a lot of other tribes, and the goal covers them all.

Not quite. The text says all the rest of the Israelites were of one mind to make David king (1 Chronicles 12:38). That's the opposite of divided. It's rare to get a whole nation to agree on anything. I can't even get my bakers to agree on a topping.
False is right. The text says, “…all the rest of the Israelites were of one mind to make David king.” (1 Chronicles 12:38). One mind, friend. There's no argument in that sentence.

True. The text says they spent three days eating and drinking with David, “for their relatives had provided for them.” (1 Chronicles 12:39). Somebody back home did the packing and the planning. That's love with a to-do list.

It's true, actually. The text says they spent three days eating and drinking with David, “for their relatives had provided for them.” (1 Chronicles 12:39). Supplies came from family. Nobody went hungry at Hebron.

Joy, friend. The passage ends, “Indeed, there was joy in Israel.” (1 Chronicles 12:40). After all the soldiers and the supplies, that's the word the writer lands on. I'd say that's a good place to end.
Fear isn't how it ends. The passage closes with, “Indeed, there was joy in Israel.” (1 Chronicles 12:40). After the crowds, the food and the three days together, joy is the last word.

Silence isn't the word. The text says the people were eating and drinking together, and the passage ends with, “Indeed, there was joy in Israel.” (1 Chronicles 12:40). With all those donkeys, camels and oxen around, I doubt it was quiet anyway.
